title: The heavens declare
hook: the heavens declare the glory of God (Psalm 19:1)

segments.voice: Yesterday, mysterium tremendum, what awe is: terrible and fascinating at once, and often there all along. Your line was look up. Did you lift your eyes at a door or a window? Today, a psalm that looked up and heard something. Day one thousand.

No words, and yet a voice that reaches everywhere. That's the puzzle at the center of a short psalm, the nineteenth in the Bible's book of Psalms. Its writer looks up, and what comes out isn't a description of the sky. It's a claim that the sky is talking. Not in Hebrew, not in any language, and still never silent. It belongs to the Jewish and Christian scriptures, and some readers from other homes keep its first line for their own looking. Today, on the thousandth day of this path, we stand under it.
screen: `NO WORDS, YET A VOICE.` → `THE SKY IS TALKING.` → `PSALM 19.`

segments.voice: First, the opening line, in the King James words: "The heavens declare the glory of God; and the firmament sheweth his handywork." Declare is a strong verb. The sky isn't just pretty. It's telling something, the way a messenger tells news. Second, the rhythm of it. The psalm goes on: "Day unto day uttereth speech, and night unto night sheweth knowledge." Each day hands the message to the next day, each night to the next night, like a relay that has never stopped. You didn't miss the start; it's still going. Third, the riddle. The King James reads: "There is no speech nor language, where their voice is not heard." Some readers hear the Hebrew differently: there is no speech, there are no words, their voice is not heard. And yet, the next verse says, it goes out through all the earth. A speech made of no words at all. That may be why it reaches everyone: nobody needs a translation. Fourth, the turn. Halfway through, the psalm moves from the sky to the teaching: "The law of the LORD is perfect, converting the soul". The same writer reads two books, the heavens above and the words in hand, and finds them saying something alike. For someone on this path, of any faith or none, the first book is open every evening. You don't have to agree with what it says to stand still and listen.
screen: `THE SKY IS TELLING SOMETHING.` · `DAY UNTO DAY, NIGHT UNTO NIGHT.` · `A SPEECH WITH NO WORDS.` · `TWO BOOKS: SKY AND TEACHING.` · then, large: `THE HEAVENS DECLARE.`

segments.voice: If you can, look at the sky now, through a window or outside. If it's night, find what's there: a star, a plane, the glow of the town on the clouds. If it's day, the blue or the gray, and how far it goes. Settle the breath. Don't try to name the clouds or read the weather. Just listen with your eyes, the way you'd listen to someone who speaks a language you don't know: not the words, the tone. What is the sky saying today, without saying anything? If you pray, you can say the psalm's first line quietly and leave the rest to the sky. The bell holds the time.
Firmament. The sky itself, which the psalm says shows God's handiwork and speaks, day to day and night to night, with no words. Today's word.
Your line: day unto day uttereth speech. Tonight, find one star or one light in the sky, and before you look away, ask what it was telling. Day one thousand.

howItsDone: Psalm 19 is prayed in Jewish and Christian worship; some people on other paths read its first line outdoors, at sunrise or under the night sky.

notes: howItsDone says Psalm 19 is prayed in Jewish and Christian worship (e.g. Shabbat morning Pesukei de-Zimra; Christian daily offices): confirm.
Psalm 19:3 alternative reading (no speech, no words, voice not heard) is attributed to 'some readers'; the KJV supplies 'where' in italics. A Hebraist should confirm.
Hebrew verse numbering differs (the superscription is verse 1, so 'the heavens declare' is 19:2 in Hebrew Bibles); the original-game note avoids the number. Check Hebrew spelling and transliteration.
Day 1000 is mentioned once in the hook without fanfare.
Audit: hook said the writer 'is outside', which the psalm does not say; now 'looks up'.
Editor: carry changed from watching dusk or dawn to one star or light tonight, so it doesn't repeat day 1006's carry (watch one turn of the day).
